title: Challenge: Group by Canonical Key

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only group-by-key program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Anagrams have the same sorted multiset of letters. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[abc,bca,foo]`, the worked program returns `2`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[eat,tea,tan,ate,nat]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Group words by sorted letters and return the size of the largest group.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Group words by sorted letters and return the size of the largest group. On input `[eat,tea,tan,ate,nat]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Transform each item to a stable key and collect items sharing that key. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A key-derived representation lets later work reuse an earlier fact. It may be a set, a map from keys to state, compressed ranks, or a rolling fingerprint; name which one this pattern uses. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(sum of L log L) letter-key sorting · O(total symbols) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Check missing keys, repeated keys, and collisions conceptually; expected constant-time operations are not a worst-case promise. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `1`. Anagrams have the same sorted multiset of letters. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: eat, tea, and ate all produce the key [a,e,t]. tan and nat produce [a,n,t]. The largest group therefore contains 3 words, even though the groups may be iterated in a different order.
